1972-40.work: I drew this jar’s blue band like a ladder. A child asked where the rungs ended. That was the evening I fetched the upper photograph.
1972-40.comparison: The band bends around the opening. The tall panels in the standing view belong lower down.
1972-40.rail: I post the unloading sketches in a hurry. With both views open, I can point to the band without borrowing a panel from the body.
1972-40.railDone: That blue line now leads my eye around the rim. I can show the opening and the panels before my next round.
1972-40.pocket: The bend is what I want to see. On my small table, the standing jar can be the cover I return to after lifting the flap.
1972-40.pocketDone: I followed the blue round the opening. When I shut the flap, the tall panels were still there lower down.
1972-40.revisit: A carrier drew our rim mark as a flat ladder, too. Give the two photographs room for their own directions.
1972-40.boardDone: A reader at the board can follow the round band and then pick out the panels below it.
1972-40.deskDone: From the aisle you see the panels. Follow the tab to the desk to trace the rim and keep both drawings in view.
1972-40.hintAtCase: Follow the blue band until the jar hides it. The other photograph picks it up again.
1972-40.hintAtReturn: At Marek’s table, a reader facing the panels needs a way to find the circle above them.
1972-40.journal: I followed the blue band round the storage jar. It looked like a ladder until the second view let me see where the line went.

1989-357.work: I put a dot over each duck on the old sleeve. From that end the dots nearly touched. The other end gives those heads some room.
1989-357.comparison: The far view makes space between the two raised heads. It also brings the rim out from behind them.
1989-357.rail: Two helpers are picking cases from a long shelf. Leave them one place to count the heads and check the rim.
1989-357.railDone: From my side of the rail, the gap between the heads stays clear. I can call both marks to the helper beside me.
1989-357.pocket: I read very close to the glass. Let me lift the far end to see where the rim sits when the two heads separate.
1989-357.pocketDone: I can take the two heads apart with my eyes now. The cover still shows why they looked so close together.
1989-357.revisit: Someone has put one duck on the trail card. The nearer sleeve shows the cramped view that may have led them there.
1989-357.boardDone: At the board, both approaches give the pair enough space to count. The rim has its own line.
1989-357.deskDone: The aisle sleeve preserves the crowded view. The desk gives the two heads room, with the same case number beside them.
1989-357.hintAtCase: Keep one duck head in view while you turn the glass. What comes clear behind its neighbour?
1989-357.hintAtReturn: Approach the sleeves from the other end. See whether the second head still shares an outline with the rim.
1989-357.journal: My drawing of the duck jar nearly joined the two heads. I found the space between them when I looked down past the rim.

1989-360.work: A visitor asked why the dragon was missing when she looked into the cup. I’d used the outside as the cover for both photographs.
1989-360.comparison: The standing cup shows the stem and patterned wall. From above the small group sits at the centre, within its own painted space.
1989-360.rail: I carry a copy for the window crew. They need to point somebody to the stem or the centre without talking through the same mouthful of names.
1989-360.railDone: I’ve set a finger under the stem in one frame and at the centre of the other. The crew can choose which view to hand over.
1989-360.pocket: Let the cup stand on my outer leaf. I can bring the little centre painting into the lamplight once I have the whole rim in mind.
1989-360.pocketDone: The flap brought the centre into reach. The narrow stem is waiting on the outside when the cover comes down.
1989-360.revisit: A reader may take the centre picture for the entire decoration. Keep the inner and outer positions plain on this board.
1989-360.boardDone: The board shows which marks belong inside and which run around the wall. Two people can point at different views at once.
1989-360.deskDone: The standing profile gives an aisle reader enough to identify the cup. The desk is where its centre comes into view.
1989-360.hintAtCase: Peer into the cup. The decoration on the wall of the cup gives way to a little group in the middle.
1989-360.hintAtReturn: Someone approaching the cup from above will meet the middle first. Give the outside decoration a place too.
1989-360.journal: I could fit the stem cup on one slip. Its tiny scene in the centre needed a view of its own.

1973-13.work: Our drawer sketch ended at a flat line. I was the one who drew it. The jar’s foot has an inside that my line left blank.
1973-13.comparison: The taper ends at a narrow foot. Look from below and the middle of that round foot is recessed.
1973-13.rail: I’m matching two cards before the shelves close. Keep the recess within sight of the flaring rim so I can carry the right card.
1973-13.railDone: That hollow belongs to this jar’s foot. I can check the tapered side and the ring without guessing from my floor sketch.
1973-13.pocket: The recess is hard to trace with the broad jar beside my ink. I’ll open the lower view when the light reaches the hinge.
1973-13.pocketDone: The inset round area is clear. The jar’s flare still has a place on the folded cover after I check it.
1973-13.revisit: We write depths beside pits here. The recess under this foot needs the same care when we show where the profile ends.
1973-13.boardDone: The side stays upright next to the view from below. A reader can find the step in the foot without picturing the jar upside down.
1973-13.deskDone: The aisle keeps the taper and the foot outline. At the desk the hollow has its own larger space.
1973-13.hintAtCase: Where does the jar meet the shelf? Look under that spot in the other view.
1973-13.hintAtReturn: The wide mouth tells a carrier very little about the foot. Try giving the underside its own approach.
1973-13.journal: I had the outline of the jar’s foot. Turning to the underside gave me the hollow my outline had missed.

1989-366.work: The old sleeve calls this vase ‘even at either end’. My hand wrote that. The mouth and the base should have their own say.
1989-366.comparison: The neck flares into an uneven rim. The second photograph is filled by the wide flat underside.
1989-366.rail: A courier sketched the flare where I needed the base. Put both shapes together so I can correct the note before it travels.
1989-366.railDone: My note now sends readers to the flat underside for the base. It gives the irregular mouth a different mark.
1989-366.pocket: I can rest my pencil along the neck in the standing view. The lower leaf will give me room to check the base separately.
1989-366.pocketDone: I found the flat area without losing the long neck. I can turn the pocket back to the rough rim when someone asks where we began.
1989-366.revisit: A storekeeper wants a foot silhouette for our tray. Keep that far from the irregular outline at the mouth.
1989-366.boardDone: From the board, the foot silhouette is available to the tray maker and the flared mouth is still easy to point to.
1989-366.deskDone: I left the full vase in the aisle. The foot silhouette is at the desk, ready for someone who needs the lower view.
1989-366.hintAtCase: The narrow neck pulls the eye upward. The glass can take you all the way round to the broad place the vase rests on.
1989-366.hintAtReturn: One traveller sees the uneven lip. From across the table another can check the base that supports it.
1989-366.journal: I put the Khmer vase’s uneven mouth beside its flat underside. They make surprisingly different silhouettes for one piece.

1983-156.work: A child drew this fruit with a stem. When I said ‘loop’, she asked whether the whole top came apart. I had to send for the other print.
1983-156.comparison: The pale loop belongs to the lid. In the separated view, the vessel has a circular mouth of its own.
1983-156.rail: Our next case slip has one line for the jar. Give me room to show the lid and body without making a second museum number.
1983-156.railDone: I can point to both parts under the one accession. My slip no longer sends anyone looking for a second vessel.
1983-156.pocket: On the outside it looks like one neat fruit. Under the flap I can mark the looped lid and the circle that it covered.
1983-156.pocketDone: I’ve left a small line between lid and mouth on the inner leaf. The cover keeps them together as one jar.
1983-156.revisit: We keep the assembled sketch near the arrival turn. Let the parted shape appear under the same label with a clear break between pieces.
1983-156.boardDone: The two drawings give readers the fruit shape and the uncovered mouth. Both stay under the jar’s record.
1983-156.deskDone: The assembled fruit marks the way to the desk. There the loop and the circular opening can be checked on separate leaves.
1983-156.hintAtCase: Keep track of the loop as the fruit opens. Which piece takes the loop with it?
1983-156.hintAtReturn: Marek has two pockets. Leave enough space for someone to put the loop back with the lid.
1983-156.journal: My first sketch made the loop on the fruit-shaped jar’s lid look like its mouth. The open view gave each part its own place.

1917-26.work: I trimmed a picture to fit a card and all anybody remembered was blue. The pale half of this cloth deserves a place on the next card.
1917-26.comparison: The close view picks out stems and blossoms on the blue field. The spread cloth shows where that field meets the pale pattern.
1917-26.rail: People leaving the racks want one look at where the colours change. Spread the close view where I can still see that join.
1917-26.railDone: I can lead the eye from the pale field to the blossoms on the blue. The detail stays with the part of the cloth it came from.
1917-26.pocket: My lamp makes the pale stems plain. Give the blue field an inside leaf so I can point back to the change in colour when I close it.
1917-26.pocketDone: I found the blossoms and put the pale field back in sight. The hinge lets me keep both without folding the full picture to fit.
1917-26.revisit: A guide will walk along our board as if it were a long cloth. Put a mark at the colour change to tell them where this inset belongs.
1917-26.boardDone: The board puts flowers inside the dark field and leaves the join to the pale field in reach.
1917-26.deskDone: The spread cloth stays on the board. The desk has the blossom close-up, with a tab back to the blue side.
1917-26.hintAtCase: Find the line where the cloth turns dark blue. Start looking for the stems on that side.
1917-26.hintAtReturn: A blossom fills the shutter. Pull back until a reader can find its blue panel again.
1917-26.journal: I found the little blossoms in the sarong after tracing the pale field to the blue. A close crop alone would have left me hunting for them.

1925-477.work: I let the mount hide the edge of this narrow strip. The first question at the rail was about the lines my clamp had covered.
1925-477.comparison: The long strip gives the pattern its run. The closer edge shows small straight repeats beside the figure.
1925-477.rail: I need the length and the edge to fit one look before I carry the picture back. Give the figure room beside the repeats.
1925-477.railDone: Readers can find the fine lines at the edge without mistaking the cropped patch for the whole length.
1925-477.pocket: At my little desk the strip would run into the coat hooks. I can lift the repeat photograph over one end of the long outline.
1925-477.pocketDone: I held the view of the repeated lines under the lamp and then found that edge again on the spread cloth.
1925-477.revisit: Keep the edge inset where a reader can move from the long strip to the short straight lines in one step.
1925-477.boardDone: The board’s line takes you from the figure to the border repeats. A reader can point from a distance.
1925-477.deskDone: The board leaves the long outline clear. At the desk the close lines are large enough for a reader to trace beside the matching edge.
1925-477.hintAtCase: Start at the edge of the long strip. Tiny straight marks there become visible when you bring the cloth nearer in the glass.
1925-477.hintAtReturn: If a reader can see the small lines but has lost the strip, bring its long edge back into the frame.
1925-477.journal: I could follow the brocade for its whole length. Its finest straight lines came into focus only when I stopped at the edge.

1917-770.work: Two children took the missing pattern for a worn patch. I’d hung only the decorated side of the Bagobo backpack. Bring that first sleeve back after you turn it.
1917-770.comparison: Long cords hang above the patterned panel. The other face is plainer and shows its own vertical lines.
1917-770.rail: Someone at the rail wants to match pictures of a single bag. Let the cords steady the comparison while I check the change in pattern.
1917-770.railDone: The two faces belong to the same backpack. A reader can pick out the cords and see which face carries the more prominent pattern.
1917-770.pocket: Keep the cords on the cover. When I lift the leaf to check the plainer face, that gives me a place to come back to.
1917-770.pocketDone: I can see the upright lines on the plainer side. I kept the flap’s number with the cords so nobody files a second bag.
1917-770.revisit: People at this junction ask ‘which side?’ before they ask ‘whose bag?’ Keep the Bagobo attribution next to the turn between sleeves.
1917-770.boardDone: From either end of the board we can find the same bag. The face with the pattern and the face with the upright lines have each kept their place.
1917-770.deskDone: The patterned view in the aisle names the bag. The desk keeps the other face and its vertical lines in the same numbered pair.
1917-770.hintAtCase: The cords give you a landmark while the Bagobo backpack turns. Follow what changes below them.
1917-770.hintAtReturn: A visitor has seen the patterned panel. Give the plain, lined face its own sleeve before describing the whole bag.
1917-770.journal: I kept the long cords in sight while I checked the plainer face of the Bagobo backpack. Both sides travelled under one case number.

1934-330.work: I wrote ‘shawl’ on the lid of this case. A visitor looked for the rest of it in my drawer. We have a border fragment with two faces.
1934-330.comparison: The three curved shapes can be followed on each face. The darker side leaves their outlines visible.
1934-330.rail: I can show the same three curves to the next group while they stand together. Leave room to say ‘fragment’ before they carry the picture away.
1934-330.railDone: The curves match from both sides of this piece. The little hold on my rail keeps the word ‘fragment’ with them.
1934-330.pocket: I can turn the darker face towards the lamp. The sleeve will need a name for what stays in my hand after I close it.
1934-330.pocketDone: I counted the three curves in the shade and found them in colour again. The cover calls this a border fragment.
1934-330.revisit: We have empty spans on our route board too. Keep some blank beside this border so no one thinks our photographs supply the shawl.
1934-330.boardDone: A reader can follow the outlines across two faces of the remnant. There is open space where the unpictured cloth would need its own records.
1934-330.deskDone: The aisle names the remnant. The desk holds the darker face for anyone trying to follow those three curves.
1934-330.hintAtCase: Pick one of the three curves in the shawl border. Try finding its outline on the darker face.
1934-330.hintAtReturn: Carry the curve across the two sleeves. Its outline may help a reader match the faces when their colours differ.
1934-330.journal: I traced three curves through the shawl fragment, then found them on its darker face. The missing length stayed missing.

1952-190.work: When I work past supper I start calling one end the other. This shawl’s long blue centre is the part that gets me home.
1952-190.comparison: The tight rows sit at a patterned end. The broad blue centre separates it from the far end.
1952-190.rail: I have to explain the length to the people on the far side of the rail. Give them a landmark for the little rows.
1952-190.railDone: From the blue centre I can take a group straight to the checked end. The other end stays visible in the long view.
1952-190.pocket: The small rows need a closer lamp than the full shawl. Leave the long blue field outside so I can find my place again.
1952-190.pocketDone: I counted rows on the end photograph and put them back at the right part of the spread view. The blue stretch kept my place.
1952-190.revisit: Use the long centre as a landmark on the copy. An inset needs an address as much as our paths do.
1952-190.boardDone: The little rows are findable at the end of a long blue field. I can show the walk from the centre to the edge.
1952-190.deskDone: The aisle keeps the two ends and the centre in sight. The desk enlarges one end and marks the place it came from.
1952-190.hintAtCase: The long blue centre points to a patterned end. That is where the small rows can be found.
1952-190.hintAtReturn: Use the blue centre to lead someone back from a single tight row to its place on the shawl.
1952-190.journal: I used the shawl’s broad blue centre to find the patterned end again. It was a better guide than trying to count every row twice.

2006-200.work: I kept looking for animals among the big shapes. It took a shorter frame and a seat by the cold window for me to see the small ones.
2006-200.comparison: The long view holds the long shawl’s large shapes. The nearer frame brings smaller figures and animals out among the coloured lines.
2006-200.rail: The people on the far side of the rail can see the large pattern. I need the animals near at hand when someone asks what the long shot leaves to the eye.
2006-200.railDone: Someone from the end of my line picked out the coloured tracks. Together we found a small figure inside them on the enlarged frame.
2006-200.pocket: I want time with the little figures. The whole piece can stand on the cover while I hold the small shapes steady under my lamp.
2006-200.pocketDone: The little figures show among the red and green lines. The long border on the cover is where I can start looking for that part again.
2006-200.revisit: The watchers at the map table pass each other illustrations. Put the figures’ close view back along its own coloured bands before one copy travels.
2006-200.boardDone: Two readers at the board can find the little figures in the inset and orient themselves with the long shawl.
2006-200.deskDone: The long shapes give the aisle its starting point. At the desk the smaller figures have room without crowding the shared board.
2006-200.hintAtCase: A large dark shape is easy to find. Open the closer view and look between the red and green lines.
2006-200.hintAtReturn: The small animals can fill the inset. Leave room around it for the larger shapes a distant viewer would see.
2006-200.journal: I could pick out an animal between the shawl’s coloured lines. From farther off I saw how small a part of the whole it occupied.

1916-1206.work: My first chalk note said ‘loops all along’. The sari’s edge does curl. The small marks inside the red field have corners.
1916-1206.comparison: The close frame separates the curls at the dense border from angular marks farther in. The spread view shows how far that border runs.
1916-1206.rail: I need to show the person next to me where the red field starts. I can say ‘edge’ with the whole sari and point at the curls with the close view.
1916-1206.railDone: I led one reader to the curled border and another to the angular marks. Keeping both in reach saved them a second walk.
1916-1206.pocket: If we put the whole side along my table, the end will hang over my drawer. I’ll keep an inside leaf for the two kinds of line.
1916-1206.pocketDone: I checked the curled lines at the hinge. The flat red field with its own marks came back into view when I lowered the leaf.
1916-1206.revisit: A map sleeve makes the same mistake when one edge sign stands in for a whole field. Put the sari’s close-up over the side that carries it.
1916-1206.boardDone: On the board, the curls stay at the edge. The angular marks have a place in the interior and the complete span remains visible.
1916-1206.deskDone: The desk gives the curls and angles more room. Follow the small tab from the wide red picture in the aisle.
1916-1206.hintAtCase: Follow the edge of the red field into the border. The angular marks and the curls occupy different places.
1916-1206.hintAtReturn: Through the shutter, a curl may look like part of the red field. Let the edge show where it belongs.
1916-1206.journal: I followed one curl to the sari’s border. The angular marks farther in would have made a very different sample for the next reader.

1953-474.work: A rider and a walker can fill a small frame so well it looks like the end of the story. My first label forgot this piece is part of a hanging.
1953-474.comparison: The longer frame places figures below several patterned bands on the surviving section. The tighter frame makes a rider and a walker easier to see.
1953-474.rail: The next party will see the two figures first. Can we give them a second glance along the higher bands before they go?
1953-474.railDone: The longer view kept the figures under their bands. I can take the group along the part we actually have.
1953-474.pocket: Let me study the rider up close. I’ll put ‘surviving section’ on the first leaf so it stays visible even when I close the pocket.
1953-474.pocketDone: I found the walker below the bands. The cover still gives the edge of the piece I can describe.
1953-474.revisit: We can leave margins open the way we do for a missing sheet. Give the surviving band its own position beneath the hanging’s empty edges.
1953-474.boardDone: The board marks the pictured section. People can compare the figures with the higher bands and see where the photographs stop.
1953-474.deskDone: The desk brings the walker and rider into focus. The aisle slip gives the boundaries of the surviving section and points to those views.
1953-474.hintAtCase: Keep the walking figure in mind as the glass pulls back. Look above it for the next patterned band.
1953-474.hintAtReturn: A horse and a walker fit in the close frame. Show how the bands run beyond them on the hanging.
1953-474.journal: I found a rider and a walker below the bands on the surviving tent hanging. Neither picture told me how the lost piece ended.

2020-205.work: The narrow waist is easy to copy. I used it for the whole profile and nearly filed the inside decoration under another basin.
2020-205.comparison: The upright view gives the waist and base. The overhead view shows ornament across the sloping inside.
2020-205.rail: Two people are waiting to check the inside for the crate label. If I put the standing profile alongside it, the next shift can find the same basin.
2020-205.railDone: I can point straight down into the pattern and back to the rounded base. We can carry one receipt with two views.
2020-205.pocket: The curve of the inside would fill my best work surface. Give it the leaf and keep that little narrow waist on the cover to help me recognise it.
2020-205.pocketDone: I tipped the flap towards the window and saw the inlay spread over the slope. The folded image carries the outline I started with.
2020-205.revisit: Keep the bowl’s rim in a looking-down slot. A person reading our loading sketch needs the base in a different direction.
2020-205.boardDone: The two views let a reader take the inlay across the bowl and then find the waist below it from the other approach.
2020-205.deskDone: The standing picture in the aisle shows where the base rounds. At the desk, the inside and the outer shape can be compared in order.
2020-205.hintAtCase: The bowl widens above a narrow waist. Look down its slope to find the decoration inside.
2020-205.hintAtReturn: A visitor beside the waist can see the basin’s shape. The sleeve across from them can reveal the inside.
2020-205.journal: I followed the basin from its rounded base to the inlay on the slope inside. One drawing gave my reader its shape, the other a way into the pattern.

2020-206.work: I kept tracing chevrons up onto the lid. Its other design gave me a way to stop. Put the closed container there while I unstick this corner.
2020-206.comparison: When the lid is aside, the star-like mark has its own surface. The chevrons belong to the side and shoulder in the closed view.
2020-206.rail: I can show the two patterns to a new shift if I have space enough for the lid and the closed container at once.
2020-206.railDone: The chevrons took me to the side. The star-like mark let my partner point out the lid in the other picture without opening the object.
2020-206.pocket: The lid picture will fit under my narrow flap. Lay the closed rim along the fold so I can turn between the views with one hand.
2020-206.pocketDone: I checked the mark on the separated lid, then closed the flap to put its position above the chevrons back in view.
2020-206.revisit: The map desk needs a lid tab with its own drawing. The photograph can show the dark opening with the lid set aside.
2020-206.boardDone: Two readers can see the closed shape and the separated lid at the same time. Its star-like pattern stays with the lid.
2020-206.deskDone: The closed container is a clear signpost in the aisle. The desk has room for the lid’s picture and the open body.
2020-206.hintAtCase: Look for the chevrons on the closed pandan. Open the second view to see which piece carries the star.
2020-206.hintAtReturn: The star can stay with the lid even when the dark container gets a pocket of its own.
2020-206.journal: I set the pandan’s chevrons beside the star on the loose lid. Now a reader can point to either mark and tell me which part carries it.

1986-86.work: On my first card for the Han River bottle I could find every hill and no mouth. That was a lovely card for the wrong question.
1986-86.comparison: The landscape occupies the side. The high view records a square opening and its border with the scenery out of the way.
1986-86.rail: Someone needs to check the opening against the bottle they remember by its painted hills. Give me both at the rail for the next visitor.
1986-86.railDone: I kept the landscape on the standing view and showed the other reader where the opening makes its turns.
1986-86.pocket: A whole side of scenery can stay on my narrow cover. Open the upper view where I can trace the four sides of the mouth.
1986-86.pocketDone: I can count the sides of the opening under the flap. Closing it brings the hills and buildings back to the table.
1986-86.revisit: Someone will pin this beside a river sketch at our turn. Make room for the top view so they can tell a painted scene from the shape of its vessel.
1986-86.boardDone: On the board, the two views let a reader find the scene on the side and the square above it.
1986-86.deskDone: Walk past the painted river to the desk tab. The square opening has enough room to check there.
1986-86.hintAtCase: Follow the hills until you reach an edge of the square bottle. Then look down through its opening.
1986-86.hintAtReturn: Try setting the landscape towards one approach and the square mouth towards the other.
1986-86.journal: I turned from the Han River scenery to the square opening of the bottle. I had spent so long in the landscape that the four corners surprised me.

1918-456.work: I could see the plate jut out over the foot. I promised the next shift that was all there was to see below. The underside print came in after my promise.
1918-456.comparison: The shallow plate overhangs the foot in profile. The underside shows rings where the profile only gives the edge.
1918-456.rail: A runner needs the underside for a shelf sketch. Give me one glance between the plate and the foot while they have their pencil ready.
1918-456.railDone: I can follow a ring below the centre and use the side view to show why only part of it is visible from the rail.
1918-456.pocket: The plate can sit across the crease of my cover. Fold the circles into the next leaf so I can trace them in small space.
1918-456.pocketDone: I followed the rings. When I folded them away, I could still find the foot below the wider plate.
1918-456.revisit: Let’s set the overhang against our board and give the rings a separate view beneath it. Readers should be able to find the foot from either side.
1918-456.boardDone: The foot crosscheck stays under the centre of the stand. A reader can see the rings and the overhang at once.
1918-456.deskDone: The aisle keeps the profile. The desk has room to follow the rings before returning to the side of the stand.
1918-456.hintAtCase: Follow the edge that sticks out beyond the cup stand. Turning the view reveals what lies beneath the plate.
1918-456.hintAtReturn: The side view leaves part of the foot in shadow. A reader at the other sleeve can inspect the rings underneath.
1918-456.journal: I could see the cup stand’s foot just below the plate. A look underneath gave the ring a path I could follow all the way round.

1928-179.work: I put the opening beside the handle when I traced this ewer. Then someone asked where the spout went. Give me the view from the top before that card travels.
1928-179.comparison: The overhead view puts the opening between handle and spout. The standing view shows how they rise on either side.
1928-179.rail: I need to say which side to draw the handle on. Keep the top by the profile and I’ll point while the runner marks the slip.
1928-179.railDone: The runner has the handle and spout in their separate places, with the opening between. The side still gives the ewer’s height.
1928-179.pocket: My table can take the profile. Put the overhead view inside the fold so the opening can sit between the spout and handle on one leaf.
1928-179.pocketDone: I can trace from handle through the opening to the spout. When the flap closes, I can still see both ends on the standing ewer.
1928-179.revisit: The three landmarks on this vessel would make a good test for our room sketch. Give the opening one place on the overhead view and another way to find it from the side.
1928-179.boardDone: Two people can point from opposite ends of the board and agree where the handle, opening and spout sit.
1928-179.deskDone: The standing view tells the aisle where to begin. At the desk the upper view lets a reader follow all three parts in order.
1928-179.hintAtCase: Find the handle and spout first. Looking down makes it easier to place the opening between them.
1928-179.hintAtReturn: A carrier sees the spout sticking out. Give them another angle for judging how far it lies from the handle.
1928-179.journal: My line ran from the wine ewer’s handle past its mouth to its spout. Turning the page showed how high the same parts stood.

1992-113.work: The long neck made this bottle easy to spot. When my sketch came back upside down, all I had drawn was its best landmark.
1992-113.comparison: The lower photograph shows a round base by itself. The high neck identifies the same object on the upright sheet.
1992-113.rail: I’m checking a label before it goes on a low shelf. Give me the round base next to that tall neck so I can recognise a slip from either direction.
1992-113.railDone: The two outlines belong together. I can turn the shelf drawing to face the runner without turning a base into a mouth.
1992-113.pocket: A tall picture takes up the whole height of my fold. Put the round underside just where I can lift it without losing the neck on the cover.
1992-113.pocketDone: I checked the underside as a separate circle. The neck on the cover brought me back to the upright picture.
1992-113.revisit: Somebody will walk up from the low turn and see only the short sketch. Set that sketch beside the bottle’s tall outline so the next reader can identify both.
1992-113.boardDone: A reader at either end of the board can connect the low circle with the tall shape of the gourd bottle.
1992-113.deskDone: The aisle gets the tall outline. The desk has the base photograph in the place named on its tab.
1992-113.hintAtCase: The bottle’s long neck gives you a starting point. Find the angle where the neck disappears and the base comes into view.
1992-113.hintAtReturn: If the base fills a sleeve, a reader may lose the bottle’s proportions. Keep the long neck visible at the other approach.
1992-113.journal: I set a plain circle beside the tall gourd-shaped bottle. Looking underneath had taken its long neck right out of the frame.

2025-179.work: I hesitated over the little marks under this bowl. The gift entry has two names. Both photographs need the same catalogue slip while I keep those records straight.
2025-179.comparison: Several marks sit inside the ring underneath. The gift line names Sang-goo Kong and Chang-ho Kong. The photograph leaves the marks unexplained.
2025-179.rail: When I pass the bowl card along, its little marks get quoted as if they were names. Keep the museum’s gift line within pointing distance.
2025-179.railDone: I can show the marks under the bowl and read the gift entry from its own tab. The two names travel with the record that gives them.
2025-179.pocket: The green curve is easy to keep on my cover. I want the small marks under the fold and the gift line somewhere flat to read.
2025-179.pocketDone: The hinge lets me see the marks under the ring. I can still name both people from the written gift line when the cover is closed.
2025-179.revisit: Someone on the aisle said the marks settled who made the bowl. Move the underside and the gift line where readers can check each for what it gives.
2025-179.boardDone: The board preserves the marks and the named gift on separate lines. The next reader can check the attribution without filling in a maker.
2025-179.deskDone: The aisle carries the bowl profile and the gift tab. The desk brings the marks into view where a reader can inspect them.
2025-179.hintAtCase: The outside looks quite plain. Turn the bowl over and look inside its foot ring for small marks.
2025-179.hintAtReturn: Bring both views to the sleeves. A reader hunting for the marks has to look inside the ring.
2025-179.journal: I could see the marks beneath the celadon bowl. For the names Sang-goo Kong and Chang-ho Kong I had to turn to the gift entry.

1921-634.work: I put the mouth right up against the decorated edge on a tracing. The view from above shows the shoulder has more to say.
1921-634.comparison: The opening is small inside a wide shoulder. The standing view places the decorated bands above the foot.
1921-634.rail: There’s time for one pause at the rail. Give the opening its own view so people can keep its size in mind while they follow the bands.
1921-634.railDone: I showed the small mouth inside its wide shoulder. Then I sent the group along the standing image to find where the bands end.
1921-634.pocket: The mouth fits in my little window. The outer leaf can keep the long body, so it is easy to return to the bands and the foot.
1921-634.pocketDone: I found the opening in its own photograph. The decoration still has somewhere to run when I lower the leaf.
1921-634.revisit: The map table has a ring around a narrow doorway. The vase can sit beside that drawing if readers can see its opening and shoulder distinctly.
1921-634.boardDone: There is room on the board for the small opening, wide shoulder and decorated bands. Two readers can keep their own viewpoint.
1921-634.deskDone: People in the aisle see the vase upright. The desk has the view down into the shoulder around the little opening.
1921-634.hintAtCase: Find the smallest opening at the top. Change the angle to see how much wider the decorated shoulder is.
1921-634.hintAtReturn: A carrier can follow the bands down the vase. A visitor across the table has the better view of the shoulder around its opening.
1921-634.journal: I found the small mouth inside the prunus vase’s wide shoulder. Its flying cranes took me back down the standing view.

2022-145.work: The first sleeve I stamped had room for one cup. The second was standing right there. Leave me two spaces on both slips this time.
2022-145.comparison: There are two upright cups and two exposed foot rings in the alternate view, beside the box. The catalogue keeps the pair together.
2022-145.rail: The next runner needs one docket for the pair. I want room to show both foot rings while someone else checks the upright patterns.
2022-145.railDone: Two rings, two cups, one number. I can send the runner back to fetch a matched copy.
2022-145.pocket: My drawer can hold one folded card. It has room for two little rings under the hinge if the cups both stay on its cover.
2022-145.pocketDone: The feet fit on the inner leaf. When I shut the flap, both cups are still at hand, as one entry.
2022-145.revisit: Our next reader might arrive from the box side. Keep both cups named on the shared slip and the two foot rings in reach.
2022-145.boardDone: The board can be read from the foot rings or from the decorated sides. Both ways point to the same pair.
2022-145.deskDone: The aisle keeps the upright pair visible in one sleeve. There is room at the desk for the two circular feet beside it.
2022-145.hintAtCase: Keep both cups in mind as they turn. Find the two foot rings when the box comes into view.
2022-145.hintAtReturn: A reader who sees only two rings may miss that there are two decorated cups. Let the other sleeve carry the upright pair.
2022-145.journal: I counted two cups upright and two foot rings when they were turned over. The case number kept the pair together.

2024-36.work: The pheasants almost vanished in the pale surface when I first tried to trace them. I reached for the underside and found a plain ring.
2024-36.comparison: The underside gives the base ring. The faint decoration belongs to the side of the upright vase.
2024-36.rail: The base is quick to match. Put the side next to it so the people bringing my case slip can also find the faint picture.
2024-36.railDone: I checked the ring, then let my eyes rest on the side. The next group can take the same two looks.
2024-36.pocket: I’ll keep the foot inside my fold and put the pale side closest to the lamp. A faint design takes me a little longer to see.
2024-36.pocketDone: The ring helped me identify the vase. I lowered the flap with the side back in the good light.
2024-36.revisit: A reader sent from the room’s shaded path may see the ring first. Give them a path to the side with the faint pheasants.
2024-36.boardDone: At the shared board, the base ring orients the reader. The pheasants still have a view with room for a slow look.
2024-36.deskDone: There is a standing outline on the aisle card. The desk lets a reader turn the ring away and settle on the faint side design.
2024-36.hintAtCase: The pheasant is faint on the side of the vase. Try finding any trace of that design in the view of the foot.
2024-36.hintAtReturn: Someone at the foot ring needs another angle before they can say anything about the pheasant.
2024-36.journal: My eyes went straight to the vase’s base ring. It took a second, quieter look to find the faint decoration along its side.

1963-513.work: I cut around the gold flowers to save paper. A child asked which piece I’d cut them from. The next copy will have the lid and its box.
1963-513.comparison: The closed box places the flowers on top. In the view from above, the decorated lid is shown apart from the box.
1963-513.rail: Someone is waiting to see what belongs to the lid. Give us enough rail to point at the detached view while the closed shape stays in sight.
1963-513.railDone: I can show a flower on its lid and another reader can match the closed box at the same time.
1963-513.pocket: My spare leaf is just wide enough for that lid. Keep the closed outline on the cover while I follow where the flowers sit.
1963-513.pocketDone: The detached lid has its own place. Folded shut, the gold forms are back above the body on the outer photograph.
1963-513.revisit: The old plan puts the whole box in one square. We can give the lid a second space and show the two places inside the one record.
1963-513.boardDone: At the board the detached flowers stay with the lid. The closed view next to it lets people orient themselves from the aisle.
1963-513.deskDone: The closed box points from the aisle to the desk. There is room beside the lid to check the top of the box.
1963-513.hintAtCase: Follow one gold-coloured flower as the cosmetics box opens. Does the photograph keep the lid with the body?
1963-513.hintAtReturn: The flowers may catch a visitor’s eye before the box does. Give the closed outline and the loose lid room together.
1963-513.journal: I followed a chrysanthemum from the closed cosmetics box to the lid in its own photograph. It gave me a place to start when the pieces were apart.

1972-9.work: I nearly pencilled the stoneware date onto the loose lid. My hand had already made the first dash. The catalogue has two histories here.
1972-9.comparison: The mouth belongs to the older stoneware container. The catalogue identifies the lacquer lid pictured beside it as a modern replacement.
1972-9.rail: A porter needs both parts on the shelf plan. Leave me space to read the date of the body and the later lid before the plan gets copied.
1972-9.railDone: I kept the modern lid beside its own note. The runner can read the older date on the body’s slip with both parts still visible.
1972-9.pocket: A folded card is how I keep different dates next to one another. Put the body outside and let me lift the replacement lid’s separate entry.
1972-9.pocketDone: I can see how the lid fits beside the mouth. The note for the modern replacement is still on its own leaf.
1972-9.revisit: We use one box number for a bundle here. Give the container and the replacement two dated positions inside that number.
1972-9.boardDone: A reader can connect the lid to the mouth and read the two making histories in separate places on the public board.
1972-9.deskDone: The aisle names the stoneware container. At the desk the lid tab gives its modern date claim on a separate leaf.
1972-9.hintAtCase: The mouth of the water container makes a dark circle. In the second picture, find what was lifted away from it.
1972-9.hintAtReturn: At the two pockets, let a reader inspect the underside of the loose lid and still locate the mouth it covers.
1972-9.journal: I would have given the water container and its lid the same date. The catalogue slip made me leave a separate place for the replacement.

2014-391.work: I used the red lines as a quick test for the bottle. The plain circle under the foot left my test with nothing to go on.
2014-391.comparison: The fine red lines run along the curved body. The pale inner circle belongs to the underside of the foot.
2014-391.rail: Can I get the curve and the foot in one look? A runner sees the pale circle first when the slip comes from the lower shelf.
2014-391.railDone: I showed the pale circle to the runner and kept the red curves ready for someone who came from the front.
2014-391.pocket: I’d like to follow the lines on the curve with my finger. Give the plain circle the second leaf so it can help me turn the print back.
2014-391.pocketDone: Both landmarks held their own place. The foot turns away when I close it and the red lines are easy to find again.
2014-391.revisit: We need a top and a low reading at the same junction. Keep the foot and the whisk shape stationed where a reader can move between them.
2014-391.boardDone: People approaching by the tall view can find the red curves. From the low side they can match the round foot.
2014-391.deskDone: The aisle keeps the red outline visible. The desk has the pale circle where the underside tab says to look.
2014-391.hintAtCase: Follow the fine red lines towards the bottom. Turn the bottle to find the pale circle inside the foot.
2014-391.hintAtReturn: A reader tracing the red lines might expect them underneath. The other sleeve lets them check that expectation.
2014-391.journal: I followed the sake bottle’s thin red curves down to its foot. From underneath I could pick out a pale circle the front view had barely shown.

1969-59.work: I wrote ‘the people and the tree’ on the sleeve while looking at the outside. Once the inside print arrived, I had to split that line.
1969-59.comparison: The figures are visible on the closed top. A tree appears on the interior piece in the separated view.
1969-59.rail: Two people are asking where the tree goes on a copy. Give us the inside beside the closed figures so we can point at the same time.
1969-59.railDone: The tree has an inside location on my copy. The figures keep their place on the closed lid for the far side of the rail.
1969-59.pocket: The tree can stay out of the way on my inside leaf. The figures on the cover tell me which box I’m going back to.
1969-59.pocketDone: I found the tree where the inside piece has room for it. The figures are still waiting on the outer face.
1969-59.revisit: The receiver copying our board might have to draw just one surface. Name the inside with its tree and give the closed top its own mark.
1969-59.boardDone: At the board a reader can show the figures on the closed view while someone alongside follows the tree inside.
1969-59.deskDone: The aisle shows the closed figures. The desk gives the interior tree a clear view beneath its own tab.
1969-59.hintAtCase: Remember the figures on top. Open the box in the glass and look for a different image inside.
1969-59.hintAtReturn: Keep the tree with the interior piece. Someone reading the outside of the writing box should still see the figures.
1969-59.journal: I saw figures on the shut writing box. The tree only came into view in the picture of its interior piece.

1966-24.work: The painted grass looked tall from above. My trace of the dish made the wall tall as well. The low photograph made me rub that line out.
1966-24.comparison: Grass and rocks spread across the dish in the higher view. The lower view shows the shallow side.
1966-24.rail: I have two people needing this card. Give the pattern to the one marking the top and the low outline to the one working along the shelf.
1966-24.railDone: The top picture stayed with the grass and rocks. The shelf sketch follows the shallow edge shown at the lower angle.
1966-24.pocket: I can hold the full scene under my lamp. Leave the low side in the hinge so I can follow the outline in a narrower space.
1966-24.pocketDone: The side is shallower than I first pictured. I could return to the grassy top without using it to guess the height.
1966-24.revisit: People bring all kinds of route slopes to this board. Set the dish flat in one view and keep the low profile just beside it.
1966-24.boardDone: Readers can use the broad scene to find the dish and look across to the low view to see how shallow it is.
1966-24.deskDone: The grasses give the aisle its first view. The side that suits a shelf sketch is at the desk.
1966-24.hintAtCase: The grasses cover a wide surface. Lower the glass until the rim tells you how shallow the dish is.
1966-24.hintAtReturn: The broad view shows the grasses. Use the side sleeve to let a reader judge depth without guessing from the painting.
1966-24.journal: I had room for the grasses and rocks in the high view of the dish. The low picture showed just how shallow a space held them.

1962-154.work: The lions stay with you after one look. I could still see them in my head when I traced the bottom. The photograph of the foot had its own plain centre.
1962-154.comparison: The lions rise on either shoulder. Underneath, a plain foot sits within blue decoration.
1962-154.rail: A runner is matching a bottom slip to an upright jar. Keep those plain and blue marks within sight of the lions.
1962-154.railDone: I took the runner from the ring below to the two handles above. The marks on our labels now follow the pictures.
1962-154.pocket: The lions can hold my cover open while I find the plain foot on the folded leaf.
1962-154.pocketDone: I can trace the plain centre down at my desk. When I turn the leaf back, there’s a lion on each shoulder again.
1962-154.revisit: The queue may come up behind the jar rack. Give the underside and the shoulder view different places to read.
1962-154.boardDone: Two readers can meet at the same case number by following the plain foot or the raised handles.
1962-154.deskDone: Look for the lions in the aisle. The desk puts the blue around the foot in reach of a closer reader.
1962-154.hintAtCase: Find the heads on the shoulders of the jar. Turn it until the plain foot and its blue surround take their place.
1962-154.hintAtReturn: A reader underneath can describe the foot. Keep the shoulders accessible to anyone asking about the lion heads.
1962-154.journal: I matched the two lion heads at the shoulders of the jar to a view of the foot below them. Someone arriving from either side could start with a different mark.

1999-220.work: I chose a deep spacer for this mirror. Last week I nearly used the same spacer on its flat side. My hands remembered the wrong face.
1999-220.comparison: Two levels rise around the centre on the patterned face. The other face is flatter and mottled green.
1999-220.rail: We’re passing the mounting notes along the rail. The raised centre needs its own direction when I point the next person to it.
1999-220.railDone: My two slips give the raised centre the deep space and the flat face the shallow profile. Readers can check both before copying either.
1999-220.pocket: The green face fits under my flap. Keep the raised centre on the other leaf, where I can make the contrast with a turn.
1999-220.pocketDone: The mottled face showed flat in my pocket. I closed it to find the two rising steps again.
1999-220.revisit: Our board carries a deep model frame and a flat room sketch. Label the mirror’s two heights by face so its pair can sit beside them.
1999-220.boardDone: The raised centre and the flatter face keep separate positions. A reader now knows which photograph supports which height.
1999-220.deskDone: The aisle keeps the raised pattern easy to find. The desk lets a reader turn to the flatter green view.
1999-220.hintAtCase: Look for the raised centre of the mirror. Now try finding that bump on the flatter green face.
1999-220.hintAtReturn: A visitor may feel sure both faces have two levels. Let each sleeve answer for the face it shows.
1999-220.journal: I counted two tiers on the raised face of the mirror. The mottled green on the other side lay flat.

1973-74.work: I could remember the birds even under a cloth. That failed me when someone turned their slip around. I still owed them a picture of the other face.
1973-74.comparison: The light birds and plants belong to the sharply patterned face. The alternate view gives a mottled surface with far less defined detail.
1973-74.rail: Two carriers remembered the bird. One was working from the other side. I need a rail wide enough to show both of them what their slips can support.
1973-74.railDone: I pointed to the bright outline of a bird and the carrier showed me where that picture drops out on the opposite face.
1973-74.pocket: I can bring the bright figure into the lamplight on the cover. Keep the mottled face on my inside leaf so I can check how different it reads.
1973-74.pocketDone: I could make out the light shapes on one face and the mottling on the other. The folded sleeve keeps them as a pair.
1973-74.revisit: People in this aisle remember the sharp picture first. Give the mottled face its own place so the next reader knows what they were facing.
1973-74.boardDone: A reader can pick out the bird and still see that the other photograph gives a less defined surface.
1973-74.deskDone: The birds identify the mirror in the aisle. The second surface has its own light at the desk.
1973-74.hintAtCase: Pick out one pale bird against the dark face. Turn the mirror and see what happens to the outline.
1973-74.hintAtReturn: Someone approaching the mottled face can return to the other sleeve to find the birds and plants.
1973-74.journal: I could follow a light bird on the patterned face of the mirror. I left the mottled reverse as I saw it, even where I wanted the outline to continue.

1971-168.work: Both photographs show a hollow. My first slip used ‘basin’ twice. Then the next shift asked where the ink was meant to sit.
1971-168.comparison: The decorated upper surface holds the basin. The view from below shows a different cavity underneath.
1971-168.rail: Someone is making a teaching sketch. Give me one wide space so I can point out which hollow they put over the top edge.
1971-168.railDone: The sketch shows the basin above and the cavity below. The two views helped me give each hollow a place.
1971-168.pocket: Give me a flap for the lower hollow. I can reopen it if a reader sees the lid of the pocket and thinks they have already checked the basin.
1971-168.pocketDone: When I lifted the leaf, the other hollow was under the object. Closing it brought the shaped surface and its basin back.
1971-168.revisit: We have the same problem with hollows in our route models. Give the basin a place above the underside when you set the pair out.
1971-168.boardDone: The board lets someone approaching below the model identify its cavity and still find the separate basin higher up.
1971-168.deskDone: The aisle shows the decorated top and its basin. The desk is where a reader can check the cavity underneath.
1971-168.hintAtCase: Find the hollow for ink first. Turn the inkstone and compare it with the space underneath.
1971-168.hintAtReturn: Keep track of which opening faces upward. The hollow below and the ink basin above do different work in these views.
1971-168.journal: I drew the hollow on top of the koto-shaped inkstone and then found a second cavity underneath. My reader needed to know which way up each drawing went.

1969-124.work: I filed this print with the plant pictures. Rennel asked where the writing things went. I had used the prettiest part for the only part.
1969-124.comparison: The lid gives the plants. In the open view, a long compartment and two differently shaped implements can be seen beside it.
1969-124.rail: The next runner is checking the compartments. Keep the plant lid next to the far photograph so I can help identify which box to ask for.
1969-124.railDone: The long tray has a place on the handover sketch now, and the two implements sit below its label. The plants stay with the lid.
1969-124.pocket: I want space for a finger to follow that long narrow slot. Put the plants on my cover and the fitted pieces inside.
1969-124.pocketDone: The narrow slot has its own outline under the hinge. I closed it and found the same lid again.
1969-124.revisit: People at the map desk have been filing fitted tools under decorative titles. Keep one card for this box with a separate place for the compartment.
1969-124.boardDone: The board leaves the plant lid and the working layout readable together. A reader can point to either outline.
1969-124.deskDone: The lid identifies the box in the aisle. The desk opens a view of the narrow compartment and the two differently shaped implements.
1969-124.hintAtCase: Watch the plant-covered lid move aside. The narrow compartment and two implements come into view behind it.
1969-124.hintAtReturn: Give the loose lid a pocket where a reader can still compare it with the tools inside the open writing box.
1969-124.journal: I set the writing box’s plants above the long compartment and the two implements beside it. The open photograph showed how much the lid had hidden.

2024-37.work: Someone copied the side flowers onto our top sketch. I was looking over their shoulder and missed the small hole. Spread the two views for me.
2024-37.comparison: The flat sides carry blue ornament. The upper image gives the small round opening in the top surface.
2024-37.rail: One person is making a shelf mark. Another needs to point to the hole. Both could use a place at the rail if the views spread out.
2024-37.railDone: The side panels gave me a case mark. My partner could keep a finger on the top hole without turning the sheet over.
2024-37.pocket: That little hole needs the lamp close. Leave the blue panels on the cover until I have found the opening separately.
2024-37.pocketDone: I found the little round hole on its leaf. Folding the cover back kept the octagonal outline where I could see it.
2024-37.revisit: We draw small openings in large floor plans. Give this hole its own clear projection next to the sided outline.
2024-37.boardDone: The board lets the next reader find the hole and orient themselves by the side panels in the other image.
2024-37.deskDone: The aisle is wide enough for the blue sides. At the desk the small circle stays visible under the lamp.
2024-37.hintAtCase: The flat panels help you turn the dropper. Its little round hole shows most clearly when the top faces you.
2024-37.hintAtReturn: If the flower fills the first view, ask what a visitor would need to see to locate the opening.
2024-37.journal: I followed the water dropper’s flat blue panels round to the top. There, the small opening was round despite all those straight sides.

1942-212.work: I labelled the building the ‘front’. Then the other slip arrived with a line of characters, and the people who needed the writing started from that side.
1942-212.comparison: The building is on one broad face. The vertical characters occupy the other. The catalogue supplies the Qianlong mark and its dates.
1942-212.rail: I’ll be reading the case number to people on both sides of the rail. Keep the inscription photograph close enough for the readers who start there.
1942-212.railDone: I held the steps in one view while a reader found the line of characters in the other. The date statement stays attached to its catalogue tab.
1942-212.pocket: I can keep the stepped building on the cover. Put the characters along the inner leaf where someone can look at a line undisturbed.
1942-212.pocketDone: The writing has its own face under my hinge. I can return to the building and still show where the museum’s date came from.
1942-212.revisit: Our room numbers can be read from either entrance. Use this pair to give people a way to recognise the inscription face and the building face separately.
1942-212.boardDone: The shared board leaves room to compare the building and inscription without asking either view to read as the whole object.
1942-212.deskDone: The aisle carries the steps and the numbered pointer. A reader at the desk can examine the character line beside the catalogue date.
1942-212.hintAtCase: Start with the steps on the building. Turn the ink cake until the vertical line of characters comes into view.
1942-212.hintAtReturn: Visitors can find the steps from one approach. Offer the other broad face to the reader looking for the characters.
1942-212.journal: I found the building and the characters on opposite faces of the ink cake. I carried the catalogue’s date alongside them so the next reader could trace it.

1964-281.work: The gold on this case made me draw a single square. Then I saw the inkstone has a well of its own. I’d given the next reader nowhere to look.
1964-281.comparison: Opening the case in the photograph exposes a fitted well for the inkstone. The decorated lid can be seen beside it.
1964-281.rail: Our shift needs to show what the closed square holds. I can make the two spaces clear enough to point to from opposite sides of the rail.
1964-281.railDone: One reader traced the lid and another the well. The case number stayed beside their two drawings.
1964-281.pocket: I’d like to keep the outside design on the cover. Lift the inner view where I can follow the edge of the well with one finger.
1964-281.pocketDone: The fitting is clear under the flap. I closed it and the gold-coloured design was back in view.
1964-281.revisit: Set the open photo where I can compare the fitted well to our empty storage outlines. The lid belongs beside the check.
1964-281.boardDone: Both the closed face and the fitting are visible at the board, so the next reader can follow either part of the case.
1964-281.deskDone: The outer design marks the way to the desk. The open photograph gives the lower fitting room beside its lid.
1964-281.hintAtCase: First follow the gold-coloured design on the case. In the open view, find the separate well around the inkstone.
1964-281.hintAtReturn: The decoration can travel with its lid. Leave the open well visible so a visitor can tell where the stone sits.
1964-281.journal: I saw the fitted space for the inkstone when the case was open. The decorated lid could sit beside it on the sheet without hiding the fit.

1988-75.work: Someone saw one name and wrote it across my drawing of the whole holder. I let it stand too long. Bring the carved view and the poem’s tab apart.
1988-75.comparison: The characters and the carved landscape are visible from different sides. The catalogue links Wang Meilin of Jiading to the poem.
1988-75.rail: A copyist is waiting to label the scene. I can keep the named poem in sight while they pick out the carving from the other side.
1988-75.railDone: I can point out the carved landscape while someone else reads the poem’s attribution. The credit line keeps its scope as the copy travels.
1988-75.pocket: I want to bring the character panel right under my lamp. Keep the carving outside the flap and the poet’s reference next to the writing.
1988-75.pocketDone: The poem’s name stays with its panel. I closed the flap and could still study the carving on its own face.
1988-75.revisit: Our board needs room for a reader to trace where the poem’s attribution came from. Keep that tab with the character view.
1988-75.boardDone: A visitor can find the carved scene and check the source of the poem’s name without borrowing it for the whole holder.
1988-75.deskDone: The carved view guides people from the aisle. The desk shows the text panel beside the catalogue’s attribution.
1988-75.hintAtCase: Start with the column of characters. Turn the brush holder until the carved landscape takes up that space.
1988-75.hintAtReturn: Each side invites a different reading. Give the text panel as clear an approach as the carved scene.
1988-75.journal: I matched the carved scene to one face of the brush holder. The catalogue named Wang Meilin of Jiading in connection with the poem on the other.

1991-120.work: I liked the red case so much I kept making room only for it. The paper slips finally arrived on a scrap I’d nearly swept away.
1991-120.comparison: The cord and red outline show the box closed. The open view gives the narrow paper pieces positions of their own.
1991-120.rail: The next shift sorts by what fits in a case. Give me enough rail to show the red outline and the separate slips before they make a label.
1991-120.railDone: I gave the closed case and the narrow slips separate marks. The receiver can see both beside the one accession.
1991-120.pocket: I’ve kept a whole paper edge clear for this one. The slips can go on the inner leaf while the narrow red case keeps the cover flat.
1991-120.pocketDone: The narrow pieces have room under the hinge. I shut the flap and found the cord across the closed view again.
1991-120.revisit: Some of our route slips are easy to drop. Put this little container on the board with a second place for what the opened photograph shows.
1991-120.boardDone: A reader can trace the box and find the papers beside it. Neither view needs to fold over the other.
1991-120.deskDone: The cord and red case mark the aisle. The desk keeps the narrow paper pieces legible beside that outline.
1991-120.hintAtCase: Keep an eye on the cord around the red case. The open view shows how narrow the paper pieces inside are.
1991-120.hintAtReturn: Make space for the papers beside the red case. A reader at the second pocket can see what the cord once kept together.

2020-66.work: I was so pleased with my picture of one yellow arm that I almost sent it on its own. A reader asked where the rest of the animal went.
2020-66.comparison: The spread jacket holds the octopus across a dark field. The inset makes the arms’ outlines and changes in colour easier to follow.
2020-66.rail: A helper wanted to follow one long arm from its bend back across the jacket. I can keep the whole animal in view while they trace the close frame.
2020-66.railDone: At the rail we could follow the arms in detail and use the spread shape to locate them again.
2020-66.pocket: The animal needs more room than my table. I’ll fold the close-up over the cover so I can follow those slight changes in colour near the lamp.
2020-66.pocketDone: The hinge let me follow one yellow edge. I lowered the leaf and the whole octopus came back around it.
2020-66.revisit: Make a small locator for the arms on the spread jacket. A reader can carry the close view to this board from either of our approaches.
2020-66.boardDone: The colour shifts can be seen up close and mapped to the whole animal at the same time on the board.
2020-66.deskDone: The aisle keeps the jacket and octopus together. At the desk, the arm detail has an address on that spread view.
2020-66.hintAtCase: Pick one yellow arm of the octopus. Move closer in the glass and look for changes of colour inside its outline.
2020-66.hintAtReturn: Show the little colour shift through the shutter, then leave a route from that arm back to the whole jacket.
2020-66.journal: I followed the edge of an octopus arm on the jacket. When I stepped back to the spread view, I could still pick it out against the dark cloth.
